es.text: No te quedes de brazos cruzados
es.meaning: Don't remain passive or inactive — do something instead of waiting with folded arms.
es.example: Si no te gusta cómo va el proyecto, no te quedes de brazos cruzados: propón algo.
es.exampleTranslation: If you don't like how the project is going, don't just stand there — suggest something.

it.text: Non stare con le mani in mano
it.literal: don't stay with hands in hand
it.meaning: Don't remain idle or inactive — the hands are folded together instead of doing anything.
it.example: C'è ancora molto da fare prima di stasera: non stare con le mani in mano!
it.exampleTranslation: There's still a lot to do before tonight — don't just sit there doing nothing!

bridge.note: Same idea, different hands. Both languages picture idleness as something done WITH the hands — but Spanish folds the arms shut (a defensive, closed posture), while Italian just lets the hands rest together, open and empty. Translate the image literally across and it stops being the idiom a native speaker reaches for.

interference.es_to_it: Non stare con le braccia incrociate reads as a literal physical description in Italian, not the idiom — the conventional form is mani in mano.
interference.it_to_es: No te quedes con las manos en la mano isn't a Spanish construction at all — the idiom Spanish actually reaches for is de brazos cruzados.
